🇺🇦 Ukraine’s Fired Defence Minister Demands Presidential Elections


Ukraine’s recently dismissed former defence minister Mykhailo Fedorov has called for a wartime presidential election in the most direct political challenge Zelensky since the start of Russia’s full-scale invasion in 2022.

The politician, whose abrupt sacking last month triggered a wave of protests, said that Ukraine had to “restore a full democratic process even amid a prolonged war” in a video address released online late on Tuesday evening. 

“Democracy cannot be held hostage by Russia. We are fighting precisely because we want to remain a free European state,” Fedorov said in his nine-minute speech.

Though he did not mention Zelensky by name, Fedorov implied the current president presided over a poorly functioning state that was struggling to tackle corruption despite the national emergency.

“People cannot endlessly live in a state where they do not understand why certain decisions are made. Why some reforms move forward while others are blocked,” Fedorov said, arguing that Ukraine could fight a war and hold a national poll.

“It is particularly dangerous when society develops the feeling that the main criterion for an appointment is not professionalism, results or the ability to transform the country, but personal loyalty to the system,” he said.

Elections have been suspended in Ukraine since martial law was imposed at the start of the full-scale invasion by Russia. Zelensky’s five-year term ended in May 2024 but there has been little desire in Ukraine to hold a contest while war continues.

Trump has previously demanded that Ukraine hold an election, though his once-fraught relationship with Zelensky has gradually improved over the past year as Kyiv has shown it can hold its own on the battlefield.

Fedorov, 35, was Ukraine’s digital minister from 2019 until January, fronting the country’s wartime adoption of drones, before briefly serving in what was considered to be a successful stint as defence minister until July.

But he was suddenly dropped by Zelensky in a government reshuffle after a falling out with military commander Gen Oleksandr Syrsky. Street protests followed, leading to the sacking of Syrskyi, but there was no sign Fedorov would be reinstated.

On Tuesday Zelensky formally nominated Yevhen Khmara, the acting defence minister, to take the post permanently. Khmara’s nomination has to be confirmed by Ukraine’s parliament, and a vote is expected to take place on Wednesday.

Artem Bronzhukov, a Ukrainian political analyst, questioned whether it would be practical to hold elections given that Russian bombing was continuing. “Today there is no clear understanding of how to ensure people’s safety in the context of a full-scale war,” he said.

There was, he added, “a fairly deep-rooted view within Ukrainian society” that elections are necessary but only after the hot phase of the war ends – and that the country remained “a warring democracy – confirmed precisely by the protests taking place after Fedorov’s resignation from the government”.

Protests had been taking place nightly in a square below the presidential office in the heart of Kyiv, but the numbers attending had been dwindling. However, the campaign was relaunched in a special rally on Sunday night that attracted about 2,000 people with regular chants of “Fedorov, Fedorov, Fedorov …”

Polling conducted at the turn of the month reported the ex-minister would come third in the first round of a presidential election with 13.1%, behind Zelenskyy on 22.3% and the former head of the armed forces, who is now Ukraine’s ambassador to the UK, Valery Zaluzhny, on 21.4%.

The same polling, conducted by the Socis Centre for Social Research, also concluded that Zelensky would then be defeated in the run-off election by both Fedorov and Zaluzhny. Ukraine uses a two-stage voting system.

The Dark Side of Asylums & Orphan Trains w/ Chris From Old World Exploration

Tonight, I’m joined by my friend Chris from Old World Exploration as we venture into one of the darker and more mysterious chapters of the turn of the 20th century. Across America, enormous insane asylums filled with thousands of people, while orphan trains carried children by the tens of thousands into new towns, new families, and sometimes entirely new identities. But what if there’s another layer to that history? Tonight, we’re examining a provocative question: could these institutions and mass relocations have some connection to people who disappeared from an earlier Old World—and could the records, architecture, and forgotten stories they left behind reveal something we’ve overlooked? We’re not starting with a conclusion. We’re following the evidence, asking uncomfortable questions, and seeing where the trail leads.
